config.title: Rotate Array

intro.title: Rotate Array
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function that rotates the elements of an array by a specified number of positions to the right. You will learn the core programming concept of array manipulation, including how to handle edge cases like large rotation counts. The main technologies involved are JavaScript arrays and basic control structures like loops. By the end, you will understand how to efficiently shift elements within an array while maintaining their order.
intro.usecase: The rotate array pattern is essential in UI components that display rotating content, such as image carousels, news tickers, or dashboard widgets that cycle through metrics. In e-commerce platforms, product galleries use array rotation to showcase different views of an item when users click navigation arrows. Developers implement this algorithm to efficiently manage circular buffers in media players, where playlists rotate continuously, or in notification systems that display messages in a loop without requiring constant data reloads.

objectives: Implement a brute-force solution for rotating array elements by a given number of positions
Apply the array reversal technique to optimize the rotation algorithm
Construct a function that handles edge cases including empty arrays and rotation counts exceeding array length
Manipulate array indices correctly to shift elements without losing data
Initialize and update variables to track positions during the rotation process
Integrate modular arithmetic to handle rotation counts efficiently
Control the algorithm's time and space complexity by selecting appropriate data structures

content.body: Have you ever needed to shift items in a list to make room for something new? That's exactly what rotating an array does. In this lesson, you'll learn how to efficiently rotate an array using a clever lookup technique.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
1. Explain why a brute force rotation approach is inefficient.
2. Implement an array rotation using a hash map to track element positions.
3. Determine when to check the lookup structure versus add to it during rotation.
content.title: What you'll learn
Try it
content.prompt: Rotate the array [1, 2, 3] right by 1 position. What's the result?

content.title: Try a bigger array
content.prompt: Now rotate [5, 6, 7, 8, 9] right by 2 positions. What do you get?
content.successMessage: Excellent! Rotating right by 2 gives us [8, 9, 5, 6, 7].

content.title: One more
content.successMessage: Great work! You manually shifted elements to get [40, 50, 60, 10, 20, 30].

content.body: What you just did was a manual rotation - you visually tracked where each element should move. For small arrays this works, but for larger arrays we need a systematic approach.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When arrays have thousands of elements, manually tracking positions becomes impossible. We need a method that works for any size. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: The core idea is to remember what we've already seen. Instead of manually shifting each element, we can use a lookup structure (like an object or Map) to track where each element should end up after rotation.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Think of it like a notebook where we write down what we've seen and check it in one step. For rotation, we write down where each element's new position will be.

content.body: We'll calculate each element's new position using modular arithmetic and store it in a lookup structure.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
For array [1,2,3,4,5] rotated right by 2:
1. New position for index 0: (0+2)%5 = 2 → store 1 at position 2
2. New position for index 1: (1+2)%5 = 3 → store 2 at position 3
3. New position for index 2: (2+2)%5 = 4 → store 3 at position 4
4. New position for index 3: (3+2)%5 = 0 → store 4 at position 0
5. New position for index 4: (4+2)%5 = 1 → store 5 at position 1
Result: [4,5,1,2,3]

content.body:
1. Create an empty array for the result
2. For each element in the original array:
   a. Calculate its new position: (current index + rotation) % array length
   b. Place the element at that new position in the result array
3. Return the rotated array
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up the function
steps.instruction: Create a function called rotateArray that takes two parameters: nums (the array) and k (rotation steps). Start by returning an empty array for now.
steps.hint: Remember function syntax: function rotateArray(nums, k) { }

steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure you're returning an empty array.

steps.title: Create result array
steps.instruction: Inside the function, create a new array called result with the same length as nums. Use Array(nums.length) to initialize it.
steps.hint: You can create an array of specific length with new Array(length) or Array(length)
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close. Make sure you're creating an array with nums.length elements.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember to create a new array called result with the same length as nums.

steps.title: Calculate new positions
steps.instruction: Add a for loop to iterate through nums. For each element, calculate its new position using (i + k) % nums.length and assign nums[i] to result[newPosition].
steps.hint: The formula for new position is (current index + rotation) modulo array length
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good progress. Check that you're using the modulo operator % and assigning to result[newPosition].
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's review: loop through nums, calculate newPosition, and assign the value to result.

steps.title: Return the result
steps.instruction: Finally, return the result array instead of the empty array.
steps.hint: Simply change what you're returning from [] to result
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've completed the rotateArray function.

steps.feedbackWrong: Remember to return result instead of an empty array.

content.body: Great job! You've learned how to rotate an array efficiently using position calculation. Remember: the key insight was calculating new positions with (i + k) % length and storing elements directly in their final spots. This approach avoids unnecessary shifting and works for arrays of any size.
content.title: Done
